Unity is Canceling the Runtime Fee
$0.20 per install, even if your app is free, is insane. Unreal and Godot are serious competitors now. I dont see how Unity thinks this will work.
It reminds me of Darth Vader's line: 'I have altered the deal. Pray I don't alter it further.' The per-install fee applies retroactively to games built on Unity even before this was announced.

I think they plan on including spyware that calls home to Unity when a game is installed. Despite being terrible, this is much easier for them than relying on or forcing developers to accurately report sales.

I used XNA, then MS killed it... then switched to Unity, been using it since 2012... As a lone indie dev I find Unreal very tedious and slow to use, but Unity/Godot you just sit down and start writing C# code and can ignore the engine features.

(President of VideoLAN) We've had discussions for years with Apple, Google, Windows stores. It's always challenging, but Unity was a headache an order of magnitude bigger: no answers, 3 different answers contradicting each other, and plain bad faith.

Unity basically told us we were not welcome back to their Store, ever, even if we removed all LGPL code. Yet there are currently hundreds of Unity assets that include LGPL dependencies like FFmpeg still in the Store—enforcement is seemingly random.

Unity's mishandling of the Runtime Fee policy announcement has caused permanent damage to their reputation. I follow a lot of game developers online. Every single one that uses Unity today is planning to switch engines for their future games.
Even before the drama, Unity was a sinking ship that was not profitable. Something will have to give eventually.

As a game developer and Unity user, I was concerned about the new pricing model, however after actually reading the changes, 99% of developers are not affected, and in some cases still cheaper than Unreal.

What Unity offers is a solid way to build cross platform and target iOS. They're able to offer that because they have the resources to keep up with iOS; open-source alternatives struggle to keep on the iOS treadmill.
I've been watching gamedev streamers port their games to Godot and it's clear that it's not there yet in terms of feature parity—some major things like profiling are miles off still.

Unity forced my last company into the more expensive license unilaterally and with no discussion. They doubled our costs just because they can. At this point, we should all treat Unity like we do Broadcom—utterly toxic.

The extravagant cost of a Unity seat meant we couldn't afford to give anyone except the Unity devs a license... For the same reason, we couldn't set up a build server in our CI system. It was an absolute nightmare.
I switched to unreal several years ago because Unity had written hundreds of gigabytes of log files complaining that it could not phone home and filled up my hard drive.

This shows once again that Unity is an unreliable option for new projects. The worst part is not the 4% fee, but the bluntness with which Unity has administered these changes—terms can change at any moment.
